brief.situation: 14:00 in an outpatient oncology rehabilitation clinic. You are the physical therapist. Ms. Haddad, 54, has lymphedema of the left arm after breast cancer treatment. At intake and every visit since, her arm volume was measured with the perometer. Today the perometer is broken, so an aide measured both arms with a tape at the wrist and elbow only and wrote '20% less swelling, discharge?' on the chart. She mentions her arm has felt 'hot and heavy' since yesterday.
handover: Her volume record: perometer, both arms, at intake, 6 weeks and 3 months.
Clinic policy: signs of infection in a lymphedematous limb are phoned to the patient's physician right away.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

parts.criteria: The 20% comes from a tape at two points while every earlier figure was perometer volume, so it shows nothing about change. The red, warm, tender arm with 38.4°C is possible cellulitis.
parts.modelAnswer: The 20% is meaningless because it's a different method. Her arm is red, hot and tender with a fever, so it could be cellulitis.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Call her doctor right away, hold treatment, keep the record on one method (next measurement on the perometer), don't discharge, and document why today's figure is not comparable.
parts.modelAnswer: Call her doctor now, hold treatment, measure next time on the perometer like before, don't discharge, and write it up.

scoring.modelReasoning: Track lymphedema volume with the same measurement method at every time point; a change across methods is not a change. Today's tape figure cannot be compared with perometer volumes. Separately, redness, warmth, tenderness and fever in the swollen arm are signs of cellulitis: call the doctor right away and hold the session.
